# Losakajātaka (Ja 41)

**ID:** Ja 41
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Losakajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** On the Mendicant Losaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja41
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Losakajātaka* (Ja 41) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered the tale while staying at Jetavana regarding the elder Losaka Tissa (Losakatissa-thera) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Born into a destitude fishing village in Kosala, Losaka's misfortune caused hardships to his family and community; abandoned as a wretched outcast (*kapaṇa*), he was eventually sheltered, ordained, and sustained through the compassionate miraculous intervention of Sāriputta [Fenn 1994; Migot 1954]. The Buddha explains Losaka's persistent ill fortune by tracing it to a previous life during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha: as an envious resident monk, he threw alms food meant for an arahant into burning embers, resulting in aeons of torment in hell, hundreds of rebirths as a demon and a starving dog, and a subsequent human birth as Mittavindaka [JIABS 2013; Huynh 2016]. In that previous human life, the Bodhisattva was his world-renowned teacher (*disāpāmokkhācariya*) [JIABS 2013; Fausböll 1877]. Modern scholars note that the story explores the karmic consequences of greed and jealousy, illustrating that kammic retribution is a protracted process rather than absolute fatalism, and demonstrating how compassionate external help can provide alleviation [Fenn 1994; Vetter 1988].

Automated analysis by DharmaNexus confirms five shared passages between the text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Paṭhamo bhāgo) [DharmaNexus]. Closely related versions and parallel narratives belonging to the Mittavinda/Maitrakanyaka cycle appear widely across Buddhist literature, including the Pali *Catudvāra Jātaka* (Ja 439) and *Petavatthu* (IV.8), the Sanskrit *Avadānaśataka* (no. 36), *Divyāvadāna*, *Karmavibhaṅga*, and *Avadānakalpalatā*, as well as Chinese adaptations in the *Liudu ji jing* (stories 9, 33, and 39) and references in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra* [JIABS 2013; Kudo 2004; Silk 1994; Huynh 2016; Lamotte 1976]. The narrative of Losaka was also represented visually in the Buddhist relief sculptures at Amarāvatī [Francis 2002].
